CHAPTER 2.1 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.1 · LEARNING AREA 2 · NOVEMBER

The pyramid

The pyramids of Giza are more than 4500 years old, the glass pyramid in front of the Louvre in Paris not even 40. In between there are church spires, tent roofs and tea bags. You learn to draw pyramids, to calculate their hidden lengths with Pythagoras’ theorem and to find their surface area, their volume and their mass.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • show pyramids as a net, in an oblique drawing and in a two-view drawing
  • tell apart and calculate the height, the slant height and the lateral edge
  • calculate the surface area of a pyramid
  • calculate the volume with $V = \tfrac13 \cdot G \cdot h$ and find the mass
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

The legs of a right triangle are 3 cm and 4 cm long. How long is the hypotenuse?

$\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$ cm

A triangle has the base 6 cm and the height 5 cm. What is its area?

$\tfrac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 15\,\text{cm}^2$

How long is the diagonal of a square with the side length 4 cm? Round to two decimal places.

$\sqrt{16 + 16} = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66$ cm

A prism has the base area 12 cm² and the height 10 cm. What is its volume?

$12 \cdot 10 = 120\,\text{cm}^3$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Drawing pyramids

Your folded pyramid has a square at the bottom and four triangular faces that meet at the top in the apex. A prism has a second base at the top. The pyramid comes to a point instead.

KEY POINT · THE PYRAMID

A pyramid has a polygon as its base $G$. Its lateral faces are triangles with a common apex $S$. Together they form the lateral surface.

In a right pyramid the apex lies exactly above the centre of the base. If the base is a square, it is called a square pyramid.

Net: the base and all the lateral triangles joined together. Oblique drawing: the base as an oblique drawing, from its centre the height in true length straight up, join the apex to all the vertices. Two-view drawing: the plan is the square with its diagonals, the front elevation a triangle.

Counting: a pyramid with an $n$-gon as its base has $n + 1$ vertices, $2n$ edges and $n + 1$ faces.

Oblique drawing: edges going backwards at $45^\circ$ and shortened to half, hidden edges dashed, as in Year 7.

INTERACTIVE · FROM THE NET TO THE PYRAMID

Fold up the net of the square pyramid. Drag the picture to turn the solid. Then choose the triangular pyramid.

INTERACTIVE · OBLIQUE DRAWING AND TWO-VIEW DRAWING

Change the base edge and the height. Switch at the top between the oblique drawing and the two-view drawing.

EXAMPLE 1 · AN OBLIQUE DRAWING

Draw the oblique drawing of a square pyramid with $a = 4$ cm and $h = 5$ cm.

Draw the front base edge 4 cm long, the edges going backwards at $45^\circ$ and 2 cm long. Join the diagonals of the base: where they cross is the centre $M$.

From $M$ draw the height of 5 cm straight up and join the apex $S$ to the four vertices. Draw hidden edges dashed.

EXAMPLE 2 · A NET WITH COMPASSES

Draw the net of a square pyramid with $a = 4$ cm and the lateral edge $s = 5$ cm.

Draw the square. Each lateral face is a triangle with the sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm.

Draw an arc of 5 cm around both ends of each side of the square: where they cross is the top of that triangle.

EXERCISES

State the number of vertices, edges and faces: a) triangular pyramid   b) square pyramid   c) hexagonal pyramid

a) 4, 6, 4   b) 5, 8, 5   c) 7, 12, 7

Draw the oblique drawing of a square pyramid with $a = 5$ cm and $h = 6$ cm.

Front edge 5 cm, edges going backwards 2.5 cm at $45^\circ$, centre from the diagonals, height 6 cm straight up, join the apex to the vertices. The back left vertex and its edges are hidden.

Draw the net of a square pyramid with $a = 3$ cm and $s = 4$ cm. Cut it out and fold it.

A square of 3 cm, on each side a triangle with 3 cm, 4 cm and 4 cm (compasses). When you fold it, the four tips meet in one point.

Draw the plan and the front elevation of a square pyramid with $a = 4$ cm and $h = 3$ cm. Which line in the front elevation is $h$?

Plan: a square of 4 cm with both diagonals, $S'$ in the centre. Front elevation: a triangle with a 4 cm base and a height of 3 cm. The height from $S''$ onto the base is $h$.

A pyramid has 12 edges. What is its base? How many vertices and faces does it have?

$2n = 12$, so $n = 6$: a hexagon. 7 vertices and 7 faces.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many edges does a square pyramid have?

4 base edges and 4 lateral edges: 8.

How many faces does a pentagonal pyramid have?

$5 + 1 = 6$

A base edge of 4 cm points backwards. How long do you draw it in the oblique drawing?

Half as long: 2 cm.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Calculating heights and edges

Inside the paper pyramid there is the height $h$: straight down from the apex to the centre of the base. On each lateral face there is the slant height $h_s$. And the sloping edges to the vertices are the lateral edges $s$. Together with half sides and half diagonals these three lines form right triangles.

KEY POINT · LENGTHS IN THE SQUARE PYRAMID

With the base edge $a$, the height $h$, the slant height $h_s$, the lateral edge $s$ and the diagonal $d = a\sqrt{2}$ of the base:

$h_s^2 = h^2 + \left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2 \qquad s^2 = h_s^2 + \left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2 \qquad s^2 = h^2 + \left(\tfrac{d}{2}\right)^2$

Always $h < h_s < s$. You find angles of inclination in the same triangles with sin, cos or tan.

Sketch first: draw the fitting right triangle separately, label it and only then calculate.

Inclination of a lateral face: $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{h}{a/2}$. Inclination of a lateral edge: $\tan \beta = \dfrac{h}{d/2}$.

INTERACTIVE · THE RIGHT TRIANGLES IN THE PYRAMID

Choose the triangle made of the height and the slant height or of the height and the lateral edge. Change the measurements and watch which side is the hypotenuse.

EXAMPLE 3 · SLANT HEIGHT AND LATERAL EDGE

A square pyramid has $a = 6$ cm and $h = 4$ cm. Calculate $h_s$ and $s$.

$h_s = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ cm. $\;s = \sqrt{5^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{34}$.

$h_s = 5$ cm, $s \approx 5.83$ cm

EXAMPLE 4 · THE GLASS PYRAMID OF THE LOUVRE

The glass pyramid in Paris is about 35 m wide and 21.6 m high. How high is one glass face (the slant height)? How steeply does it slope?

$h_s = \sqrt{21.6^2 + 17.5^2} = \sqrt{772.81} \approx 27.8$ m. $\;\tan \alpha = \tfrac{21.6}{17.5}$, $\alpha \approx 51.0^\circ$.

Each glass face is about 27.8 m high and slopes at roughly $51^\circ$.

EXERCISES

Square pyramid with $a = 10$ cm and $h = 12$ cm. Calculate $h_s$ and $s$.

$h_s = \sqrt{144 + 25} = 13$ cm, $s = \sqrt{169 + 25} = \sqrt{194} \approx 13.93$ cm

Square pyramid with $a = 8$ cm and $h_s = 5$ cm. How high is it?

$h = \sqrt{25 - 16} = 3$ cm

In a square pyramid the lateral edges are 10 cm and the base edges 12 cm long. Calculate $h_s$ and $h$.

$h_s = \sqrt{100 - 36} = 8$ cm, $h = \sqrt{64 - 36} = \sqrt{28} \approx 5.29$ cm

Pyramid with $a = 6$ cm and $h = 4$ cm. At what angle do the lateral faces slope against the base, at what angle the lateral edges?

Lateral face: $\tan \alpha = \tfrac43$, $\alpha \approx 53.1^\circ$. Lateral edge: $\tfrac{d}{2} = 3\sqrt{2} \approx 4.24$, $\tan \beta = \tfrac{4}{4.24}$, $\beta \approx 43.3^\circ$.

In a square pyramid all eight edges are 6 cm long. Calculate $h_s$ and $h$.

Each lateral face is equilateral: $h_s = \sqrt{36 - 9} = \sqrt{27} \approx 5.20$ cm. $h = \sqrt{27 - 9} = \sqrt{18} \approx 4.24$ cm.

TEST YOURSELF!

$a = 6$ cm, $h = 4$ cm. How long is $h_s$?

$\sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$ cm

$a = 10$ cm, $h_s = 13$ cm. How high is the pyramid?

$\sqrt{169 - 25} = 12$ cm

$a = 12$ cm, $s = 10$ cm. How long is $h_s$?

$\sqrt{100 - 36} = 8$ cm

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Surface area, volume and mass

When you pour it over, the pyramid fits exactly three times into the cuboid with the same base and the same height. A cube can even be cut into three equal pyramids. So the volume of every pyramid is one third of the prism with the same base and height.

KEY POINT · SURFACE AREA, VOLUME, MASS

Volume of every pyramid: $\;V = \tfrac13 \cdot G \cdot h$

Surface area: $\;O = G + M$. For the square pyramid $G = a^2$ and the lateral surface $M = 4 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot a \cdot h_s = 2 \cdot a \cdot h_s$.

Mass: $\;m = \varrho \cdot V$ with the density $\varrho$ of the material.

Careful: for the volume you need the height $h$, for the lateral surface the slant height $h_s$.

Densities: wood about $0.6\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$, glass $2.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$, brass $8.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$.

INTERACTIVE · THREE PYRAMIDS, ONE CUBE
INTERACTIVE · CALCULATING THE PYRAMID

Choose the base edge, the height and the material. Surface area, volume and mass are calculated along.

EXAMPLE 5 · A PAPERWEIGHT

A glass paperweight is a square pyramid with $a = 6$ cm, $h = 4$ cm and $h_s = 5$ cm. Calculate $O$, $V$ and the mass ($\varrho = 2.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$).

$O = 36 + 2 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 96\,\text{cm}^2$. $\;V = \tfrac13 \cdot 36 \cdot 4 = 48\,\text{cm}^3$.

$m = 2.5 \cdot 48 = 120$ g

EXAMPLE 6 · A TRIANGULAR PYRAMID

The base of a pyramid is a right triangle with the legs 6 cm and 4 cm. The pyramid is 10 cm high. What is its volume?

$G = \tfrac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 = 12\,\text{cm}^2$, $\;V = \tfrac13 \cdot 12 \cdot 10$.

$V = 40\,\text{cm}^3$

EXERCISES

Square pyramid with $a = 10$ cm, $h = 12$ cm and $h_s = 13$ cm. Calculate the surface area and the volume.

$O = 100 + 2 \cdot 10 \cdot 13 = 360\,\text{cm}^2$, $V = \tfrac13 \cdot 100 \cdot 12 = 400\,\text{cm}^3$

The roof of a tower is a square pyramid with a 5 m base edge and a slant height of 7 m. How many square metres of roof have to be covered?

Only the lateral surface: $2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 70\,\text{m}^2$

A brass paperweight ($\varrho = 8.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$) is a square pyramid with $a = 4$ cm and $h = 6$ cm. How heavy is it?

$V = \tfrac13 \cdot 16 \cdot 6 = 32\,\text{cm}^3$, $m = 8.5 \cdot 32 = 272$ g

A square pyramid has $a = 8$ cm and $h = 3$ cm. First calculate $h_s$, then the surface area.

$h_s = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$ cm, $O = 64 + 2 \cdot 8 \cdot 5 = 144\,\text{cm}^2$

A pyramid has the volume 50 cm³ and the base area 25 cm². How high is it? What happens to the volume if you double all the edges?

$h = \tfrac{3V}{G} = \tfrac{150}{25} = 6$ cm. Base area times 4, height times 2: the volume becomes eight times as large, 400 cm³.

TEST YOURSELF!

Square pyramid with $a = 3$ cm and $h = 4$ cm. Volume?

$\tfrac13 \cdot 9 \cdot 4 = 12\,\text{cm}^3$

$a = 4$ cm, $h_s = 6$ cm. How large is the lateral surface?

$2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 = 48\,\text{cm}^2$

$a = 4$ cm, $h_s = 6$ cm. How large is the surface area?

$16 + 48 = 64\,\text{cm}^2$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A prism and a pyramid have the same base and the same height. The prism has 90 cm³. What is the volume of the pyramid?

One third: 30 cm³

Connecting with chapter 1.2: the lateral faces of a square pyramid with $a = 10$ m slope at $60^\circ$ to the ground. How high is it? What is its volume?

$h = 5 \cdot \tan 60^\circ \approx 8.66$ m, $V = \tfrac13 \cdot 100 \cdot 8.66 \approx 289\,\text{m}^3$

A tea bag is a pyramid made of four equilateral triangles with the side length 6 cm (a tetrahedron). How much material do you need for one bag?

Height of one triangle: $\sqrt{36 - 9} \approx 5.20$ cm, area $\tfrac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 5.20 \approx 15.6\,\text{cm}^2$. Four triangles: about $62.4\,\text{cm}^2$.

A tent has the shape of a square pyramid with a 3 m base edge. It is to hold at least 6 m³ of air. How high must it be at least?

$\tfrac13 \cdot 9 \cdot h \ge 6$, so $3h \ge 6$ and $h \ge 2$ m.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The Great Pyramid of Cheops

The largest pyramid of Giza in Egypt was built around 2560 BC for the pharaoh Cheops (Khufu). It was originally about 146.6 m high and has a square base with a side length of about 230.3 m. For more than 3800 years it was the tallest building in the world. Today the top is missing, it is still about 139 m high.

It was built from more than two million blocks of stone. How the Egyptians stacked them so precisely without cranes has still not been fully explained.

Work it out: what was its original volume? At what angle do its lateral faces slope?

$V = \tfrac13 \cdot 230.3^2 \cdot 146.6 \approx 2\,592\,000\,\text{m}^3$, that is about 2.6 million cubic metres. $\;\tan \alpha = \tfrac{146.6}{115.15}$, $\alpha \approx 51.8^\circ$, almost exactly as with the glass pyramid in Paris.

Source: M. Lehner, The Complete Pyramids, London 1997 (dimensions of the Great Pyramid: side length 230.33 m, original height 146.59 m).

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

PYRAMID

a polygon as its base, triangles as its lateral faces, apex $S$

$n$-gon: $n + 1$ vertices, $2n$ edges, $n + 1$ faces

DRAWING

net · oblique drawing with the height from the centre · two-view drawing

Plan: a square with its diagonals

LENGTHS

$h_s^2 = h^2 + \left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2$ · $s^2 = h_s^2 + \left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2$

$a = 6$, $h = 4$: $h_s = 5$

SURFACE AREA

$O = G + M$, $M = 2 \cdot a \cdot h_s$

$36 + 60 = 96\,\text{cm}^2$

VOLUME AND MASS

$V = \tfrac13 \cdot G \cdot h$ · $m = \varrho \cdot V$

$\tfrac13 \cdot 36 \cdot 4 = 48\,\text{cm}^3$
